subject: Communication
title: Choice Overload: When More Is Less
description: A 60-second lesson on Choice Overload: When More Is Less.

hook.text: A supermarket offered 24 jam samples. Another day, just 6. Guess which table sold ten times more jam.

buildup.text: The 6-jam table. Sheena Iyengar's famous study proved that too many choices paralyze decision-making.

discovery.text: Choice overload happens because comparing many options exhausts mental resources and increases regret anxiety.

twist.text: Tech companies exploit this in reverse — they offer a 'recommended' plan to cut through their own complexity.

climax.text: The most persuasive move isn't adding options. It's removing them until the right choice feels obvious.

punchline.text: More choices, fewer decisions. Less is persuasion.

quiz.question: What did Iyengar's jam study demonstrate?

details.summary: Too many options can paralyze decision-making and reduce satisfaction. Sheena Iyengar's jam study showed that shoppers bought more when offered 6 varieties than 24. Excessive choice creates anxiety, regret, and decision fatigue.
details.whyItMatters: In a world of infinite options, understanding choice overload helps you design better experiences and make faster personal decisions.
takeaways: More options can reduce purchases and increase regret
Decision fatigue grows with the number of alternatives
Curating choices improves both conversion and satisfaction

faq.question: How many options are ideal for decision-making?
faq.answer: Research suggests 3 to 7 options is the sweet spot for most decisions. Beyond that, people struggle to compare meaningfully and often default to not choosing at all. The ideal number varies by category complexity and the decision-maker's expertise.

faq.question: Is the jam study finding always true?
faq.answer: Not always. Subsequent research shows choice overload depends on factors like decision importance, category expertise, and option similarity. Experts handle more options better. But for most consumer contexts, fewer curated options outperform large assortments.
